kal3: It develops as the cartilage in the hip joint gradually thins over time. The pain is usually felt in the groin; putting on socks, tying your shoelaces and getting into a car can become difficult. With exercise, weight control and the right aids, many people can stay active for many years.

kal11: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint formed by the head of the thigh bone and a socket in the pelvis. In osteoarthritis, the cartilage covering the joint surfaces thins, bony outgrowths form at the edges of the joint, and the joint's movement becomes restricted, especially turning the leg inwards.
kal12: If you are over 50, with hip pain that gets worse when you put weight on it, morning stiffness that lasts less than an hour and restricted inward turning of the hip, the diagnosis can usually be made from an examination.
kal13: Pain in the groin, the front of the thigh or the outer side of the hip that gets worse with movement
kal14: Difficulty putting on socks, tying shoelaces, and getting into and out of a car

kal16: Risk factors: older age, excess weight, osteoarthritis in the family, a previous hip injury, congenital hip dislocation (dysplasia) or hip impingement
kal17: The pain may be in the knee, but the problem in the hip
kal18: Pain from hip osteoarthritis is not felt only in the groin; it can spread down the thigh to the knee. Some patients describe only knee pain, and their knee is investigated even though the problem is in the hip.
kal19: If you have pain in your knee but a knee examination and imaging do not explain it, your hip needs to be assessed too. A physiotherapy assessment always checks the hip's range of movement.
kal20: The American College of Rheumatology guideline puts exercise, weight control and managing the condition yourself at the centre of treatment.
kal21: Strongly recommended. According to a Cochrane review updated in 2026, the average improvement in pain and function is small, but exercise is a treatment with few side effects and many benefits for your overall health. A programme that strengthens the muscles around the hip and keeps up its range of movement is recommended.
kal22: If you are overweight, losing weight is strongly recommended; the aim is to lose at least 5% of your body weight.
kal24: Tai Chi, and programmes that teach you to understand the condition and manage it yourself, are among the approaches the guideline strongly recommends.
kal26: A walking stick is strongly recommended if osteoarthritis clearly affects your walking, the stability of the joint or your pain.

kal30: The guideline strongly recommends against: glucosamine and chondroitin supplements, hyaluronic acid, PRP or stem cell injections into the hip, and TENS.

kal41: Looking after your hip in daily life
kal42: Protecting your hip does not mean keeping it still; it means spreading the load wisely.
kal43: Walk on most days of the week; cycling and exercising in water are good alternatives.
kal44: Choose chairs that are high enough and have armrests, rather than low armchairs.
kal45: A long-handled shoehorn and a sock aid mean you do not have to bend down as much.
kal46: When getting into a car, sit down first, then bring both legs in together.
kal47: Do not sit in the same position for a long time; get up and walk around every so often.

kal55: Is walking bad for hip osteoarthritis?
kal56: No. Exercise and regular movement are the cornerstone of treatment for osteoarthritis. Walk at a distance and pace that do not noticeably increase your pain; during painful spells, walk for shorter periods but more often. Cycling and exercising in water are also good options that put less load on the joint.
kal58: According to a Cochrane review updated in 2026, exercise slightly improves pain and function in hip osteoarthritis; the average effect is small. Even so, because it has few side effects and many benefits for your overall health, the American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends exercise. Exercise is one part of a treatment package, together with weight control, a walking stick and understanding the condition properly.
kal59: Do glucosamine or joint injections work?
kal60: For hip osteoarthritis, the American College of Rheumatology guideline strongly recommends against glucosamine, chondroitin, hyaluronic acid injections, and PRP and stem cell injections. An ultrasound-guided cortisone injection, on the other hand, is one of the recommended options for short-term relief.
kal61: In the hand on the opposite side to your painful hip. The stick touches the ground at the same time as your painful leg and reduces the load the hip has to carry. It is important to have it set to the right height.
kal62: When is a hip replacement needed?
kal63: If pain and restricted movement seriously disrupt your daily life despite exercise, weight control and medication, you need an orthopaedic assessment. The decision is based not just on your X-ray, but on your quality of life.
kal64: Sudden, severe pain in the hip with fever and chills
kal65: New hip pain in a young person who has taken cortisone for a long time or drinks heavily (possible problem with the blood supply to the bone)
kal66: Night pain that does not ease with rest, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer
kal67: Pain spreading down the leg with numbness or weakness (may be coming from your lower back)
